title: The SpecTag, and how a symbol carries it
text:
A SpecTag is the text `@spec <sid>`, or, on a symbol only, `@spec none` followed by its reason. A symbol carries it as a line of the comment directly above it, above its decorators where it has any — in TypeScript and JavaScript its doc comment, in Python a comment line — and a symbol implementing several rules carries several. A test carries it in its name or in a mark on it (§s-zrsc6asgmhv8tnc).

A symbol that implements no rule says so with `@spec none`, followed by the reason it carries none, and one standing first in a run of re-exports, with no blank line between them, says it for the whole run.

On a symbol, the delimiters of the comment may share a SpecTag's line and nothing else may, so that a SpecTag's text is found by a scan in any language. Which symbol a SpecTag stands on is found by parsing the file with tree-sitter and the grammar of the file's language — the parser alone, with no program and no type checker — and a description of each language names what counts as a declaration and as a test in it; TypeScript, JavaScript and Python are described.
reason: A comment above a symbol is where an editor shows a SpecTag and where a reader of the symbol is already looking. A scan finds a SpecTag but cannot see what it is attached to, so a SpecTag standing over nothing would pass it; the parser sees the symbol under the comment, and used alone it answers the same for the same file every time and is cheap enough to run at every commit. One parser with a grammar per language makes a further language a description rather than new code.

title: How a test declares the node it is written from
text: In TypeScript and JavaScript a test declares its SpecTag by opening its name with it: `test("@spec s-… what it checks", …)`. In Python it declares it by a mark on the test, `@pytest.mark.spec("@spec s-…")`. The plugin for pytest of the SpecSheriff tools, `pytest-specsheriff`, registers the mark and opens the name a run reports with the SpecTag. The description of a further language says how a test declares its SpecTag there.
reason: A test's name is a string in TypeScript and JavaScript, which a SpecTag can open, and a run reports that name. A Python test is named by its function, which cannot hold a SpecTag. So it goes into a mark, and the plugin puts it where a run's report shows it.

title: Who runs the reviewer
reason:
Print mode and `codex exec` answer once and exit, with no session around them to carry anything over. How a runner is started keeps from it everything of the session that wrote the code, so that it judges the code against the nodes alone, not against what its author meant.

A CLI held to the schema of the verdict answers in a form `sheriff review` can read. An answer that contradicts itself leaves open which half the reviewer meant, and taking either would decide for it.

A command script runs only through a shell, so the program it starts is started instead. A shell in between reads the arguments by rules of its own. On Windows, ending that shell at the time limit leaves the CLI it started running.

The environment lists what passes, since a list of what to strip would fall behind unseen. An agent sets variables of its own for the session it runs, and a new release may add more. The git hooks set git's variables to the repository, which a CLI started in its empty directory would then read through them. A variable the run needs, left off the list, fails the run instead, and the commit is refused saying why.

A run of the reviewer is paid for by the user who commits, from their own account. So it runs at the models and the efforts that user has confirmed, kept on their machine rather than in the project, which every clone shares. The git hooks read the git configuration with no agent running, and it outlives an update or a removal of either plugin. Its global scope serves every project of the user, so one answer on each machine holds wherever they commit. A confirmed setting holds its value, so that a release of the SpecSheriff tools offering other defaults changes nothing a user has confirmed.

Where a setting is not confirmed, the review still runs at its default. A commit whose review cannot be held is refused (§s-nyh9yk22ba6g77q). Refusing would then hold every commit of a user nobody has asked yet, as one committing from a terminal or in CI. The default is named with every review it runs, so that nobody pays long without knowing at what.

Whether code does only what its rules say is the one judgement among the checks, so it is asked at high effort. With Codex, high was the lowest effort tried at which the reviewer refused, in every run, a change it must refuse. At lower efforts it passed that change in some runs or in all. Nothing was measured with Claude, whose runner is asked the same effort so that the two runners judge alike. The default of the runner `claude` is `opus`, the model Anthropic names as its default, rather than its most capable model. That model costs the user more for each review. The runner falls back to `sonnet` so that a review is held where `opus` is overloaded or not offered. Which models Codex offers depends on how its user signs in, so the default of the runner `codex` is the one Codex chooses for that account. Codex offers no run without tools, so its runner turns off every one a setting reaches, and its sandbox lets nothing be written.

The runner follows the plugin a user has, since a user with one agent has no other to run. A project wanting one reviewer for everyone names it. The limit on a run's time is long, since it ends a run that hangs rather than hurrying one that reads a large change.

title: How an approval is recorded
reason:
One line appended per approval keeps every approval ever given. The lines two branches append merge without a conflict where git merges the approvals by union, as `sheriff init` has it do (§s-7unxytshhc4md54). SHA-256 is a hash every language provides. The email git is configured with is the one a commit names its author by, so an approval and the commit carrying it name the same person. The owners a node names say who reads its wording, not what the wording is, and what the reindex builds is no one's wording. A fingerprint changes with the name and value of every key in its string. A release writing the wording in another form would otherwise make a draft every node approved before it, though no wording changed.

A section's and a header's status is built (§s-9kfdycuq34beqvs), so nobody approves them. The commands refuse what no line may record, since a line once appended can be taken out only through git: no edit of the approvals passes the guard (§s-83ev4wwesbwnhnp).

A withdrawal takes back the node's approval, not that of one of its wordings (§s-5ah25f6gy99panq). An approval left standing for an earlier wording would let an edit restore that wording with the status approved. With the latest line deciding, a withdrawal cannot be undone by typing a status back.

title: A git hook runs the SpecSheriff tools a plugin keeps on the machine
text:
When a session starts, the plugin for Claude Code (§s-zh2vcr3xjumppg5) copies the SpecSheriff tools it carries into its data directory, `<plugins>/data/specsheriff-specsheriff-marketplace/`, where the copy there is of another release or missing; `<plugins>` is `CLAUDE_CODE_PLUGIN_CACHE_DIR` where it is set and `~/.claude/plugins` otherwise. The plugin for Codex CLI (§s-2pdy9gw2jrjvfb4) keeps no copy: its tools stand in its directory in Codex's cache, `<Codex home>/plugins/cache/specsheriff-marketplace/specsheriff/<version>/tools/`, where `<Codex home>` is `CODEX_HOME` where it is set and `~/.codex` otherwise. `~` is the user's home directory, on Windows their profile directory.

Each git hook `sheriff init` writes holds the lookup of those tools, a call to the script for that hook in their `hooks/`, what it does where it finds none, and the run of the project's own tools (§s-n4m5zvh96yb299p). Where it finds the tools of both plugins, it takes those whose `release` file opens with the higher version, compared as semantic versions, and either where the two are equal. The script runs what the hook is to run (§s-477gtdrkw34dzxw), and refuses where Node is missing or older than the tools need, naming the version they need.

Where the hook finds the tools of neither plugin, it runs the project's own tools (§s-n4m5zvh96yb299p) and lets the commit or the push through unless one of them fails. The pre-commit and pre-push hooks say then that no check of SpecSheriff ran, because they found the SpecSheriff tools of no plugin on the machine.

The script run when a session starts names each git hook in `.githooks/`, and each of the agent's hooks for Codex in `.codex/hooks.json`, that holds what an earlier release of `sheriff init` wrote, and says that `sheriff init` replaces it (§s-7unxytshhc4md54).
reason:
Claude Code keeps each version of a plugin in a directory of its own, which changes with every update, and keeps the plugin's data directory across updates; so the plugin keeps a copy of its release there, at a path a hook written once can name. Codex keeps the one installed version of a plugin in its cache and deletes the cache when the plugin is removed, while it leaves the plugin's data directory; a copy kept there would outlive the plugin, so the hook looks in the cache, which goes with it.

The hook looks for the tools of both plugins because a user may move from one agent to the other, and takes the higher release because it holds every fix of the lower.

A hook that finds no tools is most often one whose user removed the plugin. Refusing would hold every commit of that user while checking nothing, so the hook lets it through and says so. The hooks stay on so that the project's own tools keep running, so the notice recurs at every commit and push. Where the tools are found but cannot run, the plugin is there and its user expects the checks to hold, so the script refuses.

A hook is a file of the project, which only a commit changes, so a hook written by an earlier release keeps its lookup until `sheriff init` replaces it; the session start says so, because it runs in every clone.

title: The project's own tools in a git hook
text:
Each git hook `sheriff init` writes runs the project's own tools for it after the checks of the SpecSheriff tools (§s-pcnyfp7gev7syax). They are the files directly in `.githooks/<hook>.d/` whose first line names their interpreter, run in the byte order of their names. A first line names an interpreter where it opens with `#!`, followed by a path and at most one argument, a closing carriage return left out. The hook names each other file there and does not run it.

The hook runs them whatever the checks found, the script refusing where Node is missing or too old included, and also where it finds no SpecSheriff tools (§s-4mej6ccn7xu3d3p). Each of the project's tools:

- runs from the root of the working tree, by the interpreter its first line names, in git's own environment, so it reads the working tree and git's index;
- is handed the arguments git hands the hook and a copy of the standard input git hands it.

Each of them runs, whatever the others find. The hook fails where the checks refuse or one of the project's tools ends with an exit status other than zero, naming each such tool. It fails too where one of them changes the staged files or the commit's message, naming it.

These files are among the repository's own tools, not the system's code (§s-hheus6f395ynqvc).
reason: A repository taking up the method has its hooks in `.githooks/`, which `core.hooksPath` names, so git runs the project's own tools nowhere else. Kept in a folder of their own, they are the project's files, which `sheriff init` neither replaces nor names as changed by hand. Each of them runs, so that each reports what it would report alone. One is chosen by its first line rather than by the executable bit, which a file committed from a system keeping none loses. The pre-push hook's input names the refs pushed, which a tool judging a push needs as the hook does.

title: The plugin for Claude Code carries everything its work needs
text:
The plugin for Claude Code, `specsheriff`, carries the skills `spec`, `spec-review`, `spec-adopt`, `spec-init` and `spec-remove`, the SpecSheriff guidelines and their schema, and the SpecSheriff tools, and declares to Claude Code its hooks: the agent's hooks (§s-477gtdrkw34dzxw) and the one run when a session starts (§s-4mej6ccn7xu3d3p). It declares each setting of the runner `claude` (§s-xr5xxa9cxf2mq5u) as one of its options, which Claude Code asks the user for when it enables the plugin; each option names its default and takes no default value, so that a value Claude Code holds for it is one the user gave.

In a repository holding no `sheriff.config.json` at its root, its hooks do nothing but keep its copy of the tools (§s-4mej6ccn7xu3d3p) and write the settings the user gave as its options (§s-477gtdrkw34dzxw).

The marketplace `specsheriff-marketplace` lists the plugin by the relative path of its directory. A project declares both in `.claude/settings.json`: the marketplace under `extraKnownMarketplaces`, its source the branch `release` of the repository the SpecSheriff guidelines are written in and `autoUpdate` on, and the plugin under `enabledPlugins`. Each machine runs the release its copy of the plugin holds until Claude Code updates it there.

The plugin's skills and the agent's hooks run `sheriff` from the SpecSheriff tools the plugin carries, as `node "${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/tools/dist/cli.js"`. The skill `spec-init` runs `sheriff init` and then offers the user, at its default, each setting of the runner `sheriff review` would take that their git configuration does not hold and they were not asked for (§s-477gtdrkw34dzxw), to confirm or replace, writing what they answer and marking it asked (§s-xr5xxa9cxf2mq5u); `spec-remove` runs `sheriff remove` (§s-7unxytshhc4md54) and then offers to remove the plugin from the machine.

The skills set neither a model nor a reasoning effort, for themselves or for any agent they start: they work at those the user has chosen in their session.
reason:
An agent takes up a skill only where it is installed, and Claude Code installs and updates a plugin from a marketplace itself and runs the hooks a plugin declares while it is enabled: declared in the project, the plugin is offered to the agent of every clone and, updating itself, brings every machine the latest release.

Carrying the guidelines and the tools beside the skills, it keeps everything of one release together on the machine, and nothing of a release in the project but the calls to it.

A plugin installed for a user runs in every project they open, and a project not taking the method is held to nothing of it.

The marketplace is read from `release`, which holds only releases, so an agent loads a release and never the work in progress on `main`. Claude Code writes the directory of the plugin's installed release wherever a skill or a hook names `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}`, so each runs the tools of its own release.

A plugin is installed for its user on the machine, beyond any one project, so `spec-remove` offers its removal and leaves the choice to the user.

The user pays for their session at the model and the effort they choose in it, so the skills set neither. The reviewer runs outside the session at the cost of the user who commits, at the settings that user confirms (§s-xr5xxa9cxf2mq5u), which Claude Code asks for when it enables the plugin, as its options. A default value declared for an option would be taken for a user who gave none, and the hooks could not tell it from an answer, so the options declare none. Where Claude Code enabled the plugin without asking, `spec-init` asks before the first commit of a project it sets up is reviewed, unless the user was asked before.

title: The plugin for Codex CLI carries everything its work needs
text:
The plugin for Codex CLI, `specsheriff`, carries the skills `spec`, `spec-review`, `spec-adopt`, `spec-init` and `spec-remove`, the SpecSheriff guidelines and their schema, and the SpecSheriff tools. It declares no hooks; the agent's hooks for Codex stand in the project (§s-n76wt2bkqdmh78x).

The marketplace `specsheriff-marketplace` lists it by the relative path of its directory in `.agents/plugins/marketplace.json`, beside the file listing the plugin for Claude Code (§s-zh2vcr3xjumppg5). The practitioner's guide, the plugin's `README.md`, gives the commands that install it on a machine: `codex plugin marketplace add non4me/SpecSheriff@release` and `codex plugin add specsheriff@specsheriff-marketplace`.

The plugin's skills run `sheriff` from the SpecSheriff tools the plugin carries, as `node <plugin>/tools/dist/cli.js`; a skill takes `<plugin>` from the path of its `SKILL.md`, `<plugin>/skills/<skill>/SKILL.md`. The skill `spec-init` runs `sheriff init --agent codex` and then offers the user, at its default, each setting of the runner `sheriff review` would take that their git configuration does not hold and they were not asked for (§s-477gtdrkw34dzxw), to confirm or replace, writing what they answer and marking it asked (§s-xr5xxa9cxf2mq5u); `spec-remove` runs `sheriff remove` (§s-7unxytshhc4md54) and then offers to remove the plugin from the machine.

The skills set neither a model nor a reasoning effort, for themselves or for any agent they start: they work at those the user has chosen in their session.
reason:
An agent takes up a skill only where it is installed. Codex installs a plugin for the user who adds it and none that a project declares, so each user installs it, as they install Codex. Codex reads `.agents/plugins/marketplace.json` before the file listing the plugin for Claude Code, so each agent finds its own plugin.

Codex admits no plugin carrying hooks into its public directory, so the plugin carries none.

Carrying the guidelines and the tools beside the skills, the plugin keeps everything of one release together on the machine. Each agent installs and updates its own plugin, so neither waits on the other, and each can change for its agent alone.

A skill reaches the tools beside it by the path of its own file, which Codex gives it. A plugin is installed for its user on the machine, beyond any one project, so `spec-remove` offers its removal and leaves the choice to the user.

The user pays for their session at the model and the effort they choose in it, so the skills set neither. The reviewer runs outside the session at the cost of the user who commits, at the settings that user confirms (§s-xr5xxa9cxf2mq5u). Codex asks nothing for a plugin it installs, and the session in which a project is set up started before `sheriff init` wrote the agent's hooks for Codex into it (§s-n76wt2bkqdmh78x), so no session start asked for them there; `spec-init` asks in its place, before the first commit is reviewed, unless the user was asked before.

title: The agent's hooks for Codex CLI
text:
The agent's hooks for Codex stand in the project's `.codex/hooks.json`, where `sheriff init --agent codex` writes them (§s-7unxytshhc4md54): one when a session starts, one before an edit made with `apply_patch`, and one after such an edit or a shell command. Each holds only the lookup of the plugin for Codex CLI in Codex's cache (§s-4mej6ccn7xu3d3p) and a call to the plugin's script for that hook, `hooks/session-start.sh`, `hooks/guard.sh` or `hooks/after-edit.sh`; where it finds no plugin, it does nothing.

The scripts do what the agent's hooks do (§s-477gtdrkw34dzxw), and nothing in a repository holding no `sheriff.config.json`.

Before an edit, `sheriff guard` reads from the patch each file it adds, updates, deletes or moves, applies the patch to them in memory, a moved file taken as deleted at its old path and added at its new one, and judges each as an edit made with the file tools (§s-st6td4mua9uqt9z). It refuses the whole patch where it refuses one of its files or cannot read or apply the patch.
reason:
Codex admits no plugin carrying hooks into its public directory, so the hooks are the project's. Codex runs a project's hooks once its user trusts the project and each hook as it stands; a hook holding only the lookup and the call changes only where its lookup does, and is trusted again then, while what the scripts do follows the release. A hook that finds no plugin does nothing, so removing the plugin leaves no hook failing in the project.

Codex hands an edit as one patch, which may touch several files and is applied whole, so the guard judges each file and refuses the patch whole.

title: Where the types and runtime checks generated from the RecordTypes are written
text:
`sheriff types` writes the types and runtime checks it generates from the RecordTypes into the files the project's technical appendix lists for them. The list of those files is defined in the section of the technical appendix that describes the technologies the whole system is built with, the stack, in the rule that describes how the system generates its types and runtime checks from its RecordTypes, as the rule on data structures requires (§s-e877bnfa559tvk9); each path in it is taken from the root of the repository. Where the technical appendix defines no such list, `sheriff types` writes nothing.

A file's extension says what is written into it: `.ts` the types in TypeScript, `.py` the types in Python, `.json` the runtime checks in JSON Schema of draft 2020-12. Those checks are run by the JSON Schema validator the technical appendix names, which asserts `format` rather than taking it as a note.

`sheriff binding` reads a file of types as the system's code even where the glob patterns naming where that code lives do not reach it.
reason: Which files the generated types go to is a choice covering the whole system, and such choices are described in the stack section (§s-vj7ercem526zd6v). Defined as a list in one rule, those files are read by the tools as the levels of the domains are read from a list in the project's own guidelines, rather than looked for in prose. The extension already says what a file holds. A validator taking `format` as a mere note would pass an instant that is no instant. A project with no code yet has nowhere to write the types. Read as code, a file of types has its SpecTags read, so that each RecordType's list of code names the types generated from it.

title: What a RecordType generates
text:
From each RecordType, `sheriff types` writes a type into each file of types and a definition under `$defs` into each file of runtime checks. It takes the nodes in the order the specification reads: its files in the code-point order of their paths, and the nodes of each file in the order they stand.

Every type and definition is named by the RecordType's name with the first letter of each word raised and the spaces dropped. Each type carries a SpecTag with the sid of its RecordType, as a symbol of code carries one with the rule it implements (§s-5z5gnu7pahr82xp).

A type and a definition hold the fields of every RecordType above the node along its refines links, the topmost first, then the node's own fields, except a variant's own, which stand where the rule on RecordType variants places them (§s-nk8td3ez58gahc4); each field keeps its name and the order its node gives it, and is required where its node says so and optional otherwise. A field of type record refers to the type of that RecordType by its name, and the object of a field of type variant is written out in full. Where the RecordType refuses a field nobody declared, its definition refuses any property its fields do not declare.

A name that is not an identifier in the language of its file, or that the file already uses — the names it imports and those its language builds in included — cannot be generated.

In TypeScript a type is written `export type <name> = {...}`.

In Python a type is written `<name> = TypedDict("<name>", {...})`, every name it uses imported from `typing`, a reference to another type written as a string, an optional field marked `NotRequired`, and the object of a field of type variant given a type of its own, named by the type it stands in followed by the field's name with its first letter raised, and carries a SpecTag with the same sid.
reason:
One name in every file lets a reader follow a RecordType from its node to each copy, and a fixed order makes each file come out the same at every run, which the comparison of generated copies needs. The generator writes the SpecTag itself, so that the link from each type to its node is made anew with the type and never kept by hand.

A RecordType that refines another holds that one's fields, as the schema of the nodes says, and a field keeps the name its node gives because the code uses that name as it stands. Only a runtime check can refuse an undeclared property; a type in TypeScript or Python cannot.

A name the file already uses would break its compilation or hide what it imports.

The functional form of `TypedDict` takes any field name, a keyword of Python included; a reference written as a string may name a type written later in the file, or the type itself; and Python can name the object of a field only by a type of its own.

title: A RecordType its variants refine
text:
A RecordType that variants refine — RecordTypes each answering to values of its choosing fields, the fields whose values choose which variant a RecordType is — is written as the union of its members: in JSON Schema a definition holding `oneOf` the members, in TypeScript a union type, in Python `<name> = Union[...]`. Its members are each variant, referred to by the name of its type, and, where some combination of the choosing fields' values has no variant, a member for those combinations, named by the RecordType's name followed by `Other`: a type and a definition of their own, the type carrying a SpecTag with the RecordType's sid.

A variant holds each choosing field, required and fixed to the value it answers to, and its own fields inside the RecordType's field of type variant, beside the fields that field holds, or, where the RecordType has no such field, beside the RecordType's fields; the variant's node decides whether a property nobody declared is refused there and around it.

The member for the other combinations holds the RecordType's fields, its choosing fields required where their node says so. Its definition refuses every combination of values a variant answers to; its type gives a choosing field the values no variant answers to where one field chooses, and all its values where several do; the RecordType's node decides whether a property nobody declared is refused.

A field of type variant is required where its object holds a field and is not declared otherwise, whether or not variants refine its RecordType.
reason:
A union whose members the choosing fields tell apart is how JSON Schema, TypeScript and Python each state that a RecordType's fields depend on its values, and with the choosing fields required in every variant at most one member matches. A value that brings no fields of its own has no variant, as the rule on variants says (§s-z3dnru6qqdf9m6j), so the RecordType itself answers for it, under a name its own name gives and with its own SpecTag.

Each member follows its own node on undeclared properties, so that no node's setting overrides another's. A runtime check can refuse every combination of values a variant claims; a type can name only the values each field holds, which is exact where one field chooses.

An object with no field in it holds nothing, so the field for it is not declared.

title: The type each neutral type of a field gives
text:
Each neutral type a field may have gives, in a file of runtime checks and in a file of types, what the table below says.

A field of type one of gives the values of its own list, in its order. Where its values come from elsewhere, it gives those gathered beside it (§s-ju5vcanbjph7mgh), in this order:

- by the node each comes from, the files of the specification in the code-point order of their paths and the nodes of a file in the order they stand;
- the members of one list in their order.

| Field's type | JSON Schema | TypeScript | Python |
|---|---|---|---|
| text | `{"type": "string"}` | `string` | `str` |
| email address | `{"type": "string", "format": "email"}` | `string` | `str` |
| whole number | `{"type": "integer"}`, with its bounds | `number` | `int` |
| number | `{"type": "number"}`, with its bounds | `number` | `float` |
| yes/no | `{"type": "boolean"}` | `boolean` | `bool` |
| instant | `{"type": "string", "format": "date-time"}` | `string` | `str` |
| date | `{"type": "string", "format": "date"}` | `string` | `str` |
| duration | `{"type": "string", "format": "duration"}` | `string` | `str` |
| any value | `{}` | `unknown` | `Any` |
| one of | `{"enum": [<its values>]}` | the union of its values as literals | `Literal[<its values>]` |
| list of | `{"type": "array", "items": <its members' type>}`, with its bounds on how many members it holds | `<its members' type>[]` | `list[<its members' type>]` |
| map of | `{"type": "object", "additionalProperties": <its values' type>}` | `Record<string, <its values' type>>` | `dict[str, <its values' type>]` |
| record | `{"$ref": "#/$defs/<its type's name>"}` | its type's name | its type's name, as a string |
| identifier of | what the field identifying that RecordType gives | what that field gives | what that field gives |
| variant | an object holding its fields | an object holding its fields | its own type |
reason:
JSON Schema is the standard every language has a validator for, and the bounds on a number's value and on how many members a field of type list of holds are already named in the nodes as JSON Schema names them. Each language's own type for a value is the one its code reads without a conversion: an instant, a date and a duration travel as text, each in the form of ISO 8601 its `format` names. A bound is carried by the runtime checks alone, which run alike in every language. A type in Python can state none. An identifier has the type of the field that identifies the RecordType it names, so that a value moving from that field to a field referring to it keeps its type and passes the same check.

The generator reads a field's values in one place, whatever their source. `sheriff validate` already compares the gathered values with their source (§s-agc6fb3vx46pc23), so the generator collects nothing again. A fixed order makes each file come out the same at every run, which the comparison of generated copies needs.

title: The specification is approved
reason: This repository holds no symbol of the system's code, and every test of its tools carries the SpecTag of the node it is written from, so as a draft the specification would only stop the tests from running at a push (§s-xhcmchcngykvn2k).
